title: 100 Victoria Street encampment by-law and transit hub
subtitle: Also: 2025 tax ratios, road transfers, rural school-zone speeds, consumption site motion defeated, extra budget meetings.
overview: Regional Council passed a site-specific by-law for 100 Victoria Street North in Kitchener, where an encampment has stood for about three years. The site is needed for the Kitchener Central Transit Hub, and Metrolinx requires access for rail construction. The by-law requires the site to be vacant by December 1, 2025, and carries a maximum fine of $5,000. Council passed it {{vote:m13}} and also added $814,333 to the 2025 housing budget to help current residents move. Council rejected an amendment to lower the maximum fine {{vote:m12}}. Staff said they intend to seek further direction from the Superior Court.

Council also set 2025 property tax ratios, took over Duke Street West in Kitchener and Speedsville Road in Cambridge as regional roads, and endorsed a rural speed strategy that includes raising two school-zone limits to 60 km/h. It asked the province to keep a tax credit for tenants in tax-exempt affordable housing. A motion on the closed Kitchener consumption and treatment site was defeated {{vote:m14}}, and a request for a Fashion History Museum report was defeated {{vote:m8}}.

Council approved one extra budget meeting in Cambridge and one in the northern townships. The Medical Officer of Health reported rising measles activity and said students without updated immunization records face suspension on May 8.

decisions.detail: Council passed a site-specific by-law for the Kitchener Central Transit Hub site and directed staff to arrange alternative accommodation for current residents, adding $814,333 to the 2025 housing budget.

decisions.item: Roads, transit plan and school-zone speeds
decisions.detail: Council approved adding Duke Street West and Speedsville Road to the regional road network, received the GRT Business Plan, endorsed asset levels of service, and directed 60 km/h limits at two rural school zones plus a rural speed strategy.
Council set the 2025 property class tax ratios, with residential at 1.0 and multi-residential, commercial and industrial at 1.95, and approved the preliminary 2024 financial results.

Council approved housekeeping changes to the affordable housing property tax exemption and asked the province and the Canada Revenue Agency to keep tenants in such housing eligible for the Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit.
Council agreed to hold one additional budget meeting in Cambridge and one in the northern townships to gather wider public input.
Council defeated a motion asking the province to fund the Kitchener consumption and treatment site and approve regional support for it.
Council defeated a request for staff to report on options to promote the closing museum's collection.

Council accepted a resignation from the Grand River Conservation Authority Board and filled vacancies, including Matt Rodrigues to that board and Joe Nowak as Administration and Finance Committee Vice-Chair.

debate: Most of the roughly two dozen delegates opposed the 100 Victoria by-law. They said residents and the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness co-creators table were not consulted before dumpsters and equipment arrived, and asked Council to reject it or send it back to that table.

Delegates argued that shelter capacity is far below the number of people experiencing homelessness, that motel funding is temporary, and that the $5,000 maximum fine criminalizes survival. A legal clinic delegate said passing the by-law without returning to court risked bad-faith findings and Charter damages, and suggested mediation or an alternative sanctioned site.

Councillors who supported the by-law pointed to the transit hub timeline and said safety problems on site, including rising fire and medical calls, were a concern. They cited recent success moving King Street shelter residents into housing and new beds coming online. Staff said the fine is a maximum and is unlikely to be sought in full for a first offence.
On the fine amendment, one councillor called the fine punitive and said it does not reflect a human-centred approach. Another asked why Council would make the by-law easier to contravene.

On the Fashion History Museum request, some councillors said it falls outside the Region's role and that staff lacked capacity. The mover said the request was only to look at options. On the consumption site motion, Council did not agree to waive notice to consider a reworded version.
